content:
Hi all,

I'm Yusuf Demir, a cs&math double major student, currently doing exchange in Tokyo.

I'm starting a formalizing Efficient Matching of Some Fundamental Regular Expressions with Backreferences (arxiv#2504.18247) by Nogami and Terauchi. It decides membership for regexes of the form e₀(e)₁e₁\1e₂ in O(n²m²) time, combining NFA simulation with the right-maximal repeats of the input. The paper-specific part will live in a separate repository on top of CSLib, but the general prerequisites (that I detected to be lacking in CSLib) seem useful for CSLib itself, so I'd like to contribute them as a series of small PRs:

Automata

  1. A computable subset construction for finite ε-NAs, giving decidable membership in language a.
  2. Union, concatenation and Kleene star with their language theorems.
  3. Thompson's constructio, a finite state type and decidable transitions, so membership can be evaluated.

Words

  1. Occurrences of a word in a word, repeats and right-maximal repeats (with the usual convention at the end of the word), and a naive enumerator.
  2. Right extensions of repeats and extendable prefixes, including the fact that a prefix occurring twice in a right-maximal repeat α does not extend to α.

Later, for the complexity part: suffix arrays, LCP arrays and the enumeration of right-maximal repeats with time bounds.

I will be utilizing AI (Antrophic's Claude) to draft Lean code and mitigate tedious proof work. AI usage will also be explained in every PR decription
I think #1 and #2 are already in cslib. I'm not sure why "decidable membership" matters. Thompson's construction would be a welcome addition

Thank you for your answer and apologies for my late response.

I agree on points 1 and 2, however:

  • The first one (the subset construction) works over Set State, thus they cannot be run. I needed a runnable version to test the matcher, but I am moving that from my CSLib list and will keep it in my own project.
  • Second one (union, concat and Kleene star) do indeed exist, nevertheless only for the ε-free NA, to my knowledge. For Thompson's construction, I need εNA versions that keep one initial and at most one accepting state and few ε-transitions. I plan to keep them included in the Thompson PR.

I plan to open the related PRs in the upcoming days.
You may want to take a look at .../Automata/EpsilonNA/ToSingleAccept.lean. Maybe you can complete it as part of your formalization of Thompson's construction. CC: @Fabrizio Montesi

Hi,

  • I completed ToSingleAccept.lean with toSingleStart (basically one start state with nothing going into it) and toSingleStartAccept (one start and one accept). Both are proven to preserve the recognized language. -- maybe a name change (such as toSingleStartAccept.lean) after these additions.
  • Refactored the union I previously worked on with a disjoint sum followed with an application of toSingleStartAccept to avoid hand-made states.

I plan to open the PRs today. Thank you for your suggestions.

I have opened 4 PRs, please see them in order:

  • PR 1
  • PR 2
  • PR 3
  • PR 4

I left some comments in the first PR (cslib#1146). Do PR #2 and #3 about List currently have anything to do with PR #1 and #4 on LTS and automata? I don't see any. Will you have future PRs that make use of #2 and #3?

Done as you asked in the first PR (cslib#1146), please see my comment there.

Regarding other PRs, 2 and 3 do not use 1 or 4, and vice versa. Nonetheless, regex with backreferences (rewb) matcher in the paper needs them for formalization. But the matcher will live inside another project which will utilize cslib, therefore I do not foresee an immediate use-case in cslib itself. The matcher could come to cslib after I finish it, if you see fit.

After that, I may or may not (depending on my availability) work on formalizing suffix arrays and related algorithmic complexity results, which look a like a great contribution to cslib, if they do not already exist in the library. In that case, corresponding PRs would utilize PR2 and PR3.
I've approve PR 1 (cslib#1146). I'll go on to PR 4 (cslib#1148).
